author.name: Dante Alighieri
author.biography: Dante was active in Florence's political life before factional conflict drove him into exile. He never returned. In the poem written far from home, people he loved, admired and blamed become part of a journey through the afterlife. The loss of one city opens into a search for the right ordering of an entire world. Personal grievance, political judgment and the hope of salvation are never comfortably separated.

hook.text: What if you had to face what your life is making of you?

paragraphs: A man realises that he has lost his way. The way forward will take him through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise, among people whose lives have become visible in an unsettling new form.

Dante's afterlife makes choices consequential. Habits have hardened into environments; desires shape how people encounter one another. Some speakers tell deeply moving stories about themselves. The pilgrim has to learn whether being moved is the same as understanding what he sees.

The poem grows beyond punishment. It asks what change would require, how love can become disordered, and what it might mean for desire to find its proper object. Along the way are political grudges, intimate recognitions, grotesque comedy and attempts to speak about joy.

Read with room for both attraction and resistance. You may dispute Dante's judgments and still feel the force of his question: if the patterns of your life became a place you had to inhabit, what kind of place would it be?

orientation.text: The three canticles are Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso. Distinguish Dante the travelling character from the poet shaping the journey; brief notes help identify historical figures.
